# tulpaRatio

*a ratio with its uncertainty kept*

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/gcol33/tulpaRatio/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/gcol33/tulpaRatio/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yml)
[![Codecov test coverage](https://codecov.io/gh/gcol33/tulpaRatio/graph/badge.svg)](https://app.codecov.io/gh/gcol33/tulpaRatio)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)
<!-- badges: end -->

tulpaRatio fits Bayesian hierarchical models for ratios, rates and proportions, such as catch per unit effort, the share of one species in a sample, or successes out of a known number of trials.

The package models the numerator and the denominator as two processes with linked linear predictors, and derives the ratio from their joint posterior. The denominator is either a second response or a known exposure, and the two processes can share random effects. The ratio posterior carries the uncertainty of both components, so you can report the ratio, compare groups on it and decide which effects matter for your question. tulpaRatio supports:

- **Ratios of two measured quantities.** Families pair a numerator and a denominator distribution: counts over counts, counts over continuous effort, successes over known trials, and continuous over continuous values ([reference index](https://gillescolling.com/tulpaRatio/reference/)).
- **Shared and process-specific structure.** Both predictors take shared or separate random effects, latent factors, conditional autoregressive and Besag-York-Mollie spatial fields, Gaussian processes, temporal random walks and autoregressions, and Knorr-Held space-time interactions ([Spatial and Temporal Models](https://gillescolling.com/tulpaRatio/articles/spatial-temporal.html)).
- **Excess zeros and ones.** Zero-inflated, one-inflated, hurdle, and zero-and-one-inflated numerators are available for the families they apply to ([Zero-Inflation and Hurdle Models](https://gillescolling.com/tulpaRatio/articles/zero-inflation.html)).
- **Model comparison and averaging.** `ratiod_compare()` ranks fitted models by leave-one-out cross-validation or WAIC, and `ratiod_average()` combines their ratio predictions with stacking or pseudo-BMA weights.

The default sampler is the No-U-Turn sampler with hand-coded gradients, written in C++ on the [tulpa](https://github.com/gcol33/tulpa) engine, so no Stan or JAGS installation is needed. Elliptical slice sampling, Pólya-Gamma Gibbs sampling and a nested Laplace approximation fit the subsets of models they apply to. Every fit reports the tier of guarantee its inference carries. `mode = "auto"` picks an exact or structured backend for the model, and the optimized tier runs only when you request it.

## Installation

The package compiles C++ code. Install the build tools for your operating system first:

| Operating system | Build tools |
|---|---|
| Windows | [Rtools](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/) |
| macOS | Run `xcode-select --install` in Terminal |
| Debian / Ubuntu | Install `r-base-dev` |

Check that R can find the compiler:

```r
pkgbuild::has_build_tools(debug = TRUE)
```

Then install tulpaRatio:

```r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/tulpaRatio")
```

The code is compiled as C++17. The Eigen headers come from RcppEigen and the sampler headers from tulpa, both installed as dependencies, so no system library is needed.

### Optional: multithreading

OpenMP lets the package run MCMC chains in parallel, set through `cores` in the `control` argument of [`tratio()`](https://gillescolling.com/tulpaRatio/reference/tratio.html).

Rtools on Windows and the default compiler on Linux include OpenMP. Without it, the package installs and runs the chains one after another.

#### macOS setup

Apple's compiler needs an additional OpenMP runtime. Install it in Terminal:

```sh
brew install libomp
```

Before installing tulpaRatio, add the settings for your Mac to `~/.R/Makevars`, R's personal compiler-settings file. Create the directory and file if needed.

**Apple Silicon:**

```makefile
CPPFLAGS += -I/opt/homebrew/opt/libomp/include -Xclang -fopenmp
LDFLAGS += -L/opt/homebrew/opt/libomp/lib -lomp
```

**Intel:**

```makefile
CPPFLAGS += -I/usr/local/opt/libomp/include -Xclang -fopenmp
LDFLAGS += -L/usr/local/opt/libomp/lib -lomp
```

#### Check available threads

After installation, run:

```r
tulpaRatio::ratiod_threads()
```

This returns the number of OpenMP threads available to the package.

## Usage

1. Fit the model with `tratio()`. The formula names the numerator, then the denominator after `|`, then the predictors.
2. Get the ratio posterior with `ratio()`.
3. Compare groups on the ratio with `ratio_contrast()`.

The input is a data frame with one row per observation. The family sets the distribution of each process; `ratiod_poisson_gamma()` treats the numerator as a count and the denominator as continuous effort.

```{r fit}
library(tulpaRatio)

set.seed(1)
trawl <- data.frame(
  site   = factor(rep(1:12, each = 10)),
  depth  = rnorm(120),
  season = factor(rep(c("summer", "winter"), 60))
)
trawl$effort <- rgamma(120, shape = 6, rate = 1)
trawl$catch  <- rpois(120, trawl$effort * exp(0.5 + 0.3 * trawl$depth))

fit <- tratio(
  catch | effort ~ depth + season + (1 | site),
  data   = trawl,
  family = ratiod_poisson_gamma()
)
fit
```

The data simulate a trawl survey of 12 sites with 10 hauls each. `(1 | site)` adds a site random effect, shared by catch and effort by default. The printed fit states its inference tier.

The ratio here is catch per unit effort. `ratio()` returns its posterior for every observation, summarised with `summary = TRUE`, and `ratio_contrast()` compares the seasons on it:

```{r ratio}
cpue <- ratio(fit, summary = TRUE)
head(cpue)

ratio_contrast(fit, ~ season)
```

[Quick Start](https://gillescolling.com/tulpaRatio/articles/getting-started.html) continues with the formula syntax, random effects and model checking.

## Modelling the counts instead of the quotient

A quotient of two measured quantities inherits the error of both. A haul with more effort gives a more precise catch per unit effort, yet a model fitted to the quotient weights every ratio equally. An offset, `offset(log(effort))`, assumes that catch scales with effort with a coefficient of exactly 1 and that effort has no structure of its own. tulpaRatio fits both processes and derives the ratio from them. [Why Ratios Are Not Data](https://gillescolling.com/tulpaRatio/articles/philosophy.html) sets out the argument with examples.

## Different predictors for numerator and denominator

The numerator and the denominator can take their own predictors. The formula then keeps the shared random effects, and `formula_num` and `formula_denom` give each process its fixed effects:

```r
fit2 <- tratio(
  catch | effort ~ (1 | site),
  formula_num   = ~ depth + season,
  formula_denom = ~ season,
  data   = trawl,
  family = ratiod_poisson_gamma()
)
```

[Random Effects](https://gillescolling.com/tulpaRatio/articles/random-effects.html) covers correlated, uncorrelated, nested and crossed random effects and latent factors.

## Inference backends and tiers

Each backend carries one of three tiers. Tier 1 covers the samplers that converge to the exact posterior: the No-U-Turn sampler (the default), elliptical slice sampling and Pólya-Gamma Gibbs sampling for binomial models. Tier 2 is the nested Laplace approximation for large datasets, which integrates the hyperparameters on an outer grid. Tier 3 covers variational inference and stochastic-gradient MCMC, used only when you request them through `mode`. `inference_mode_info()` lists the backends and the models each one fits.

## Documentation

Start with [Quick Start](https://gillescolling.com/tulpaRatio/articles/getting-started.html): one path from simulated trawl data to catch per unit effort, then formula syntax, random effects and model checking.

- [Why Ratios Are Not Data](https://gillescolling.com/tulpaRatio/articles/philosophy.html): the statistical case for modelling the numerator and denominator.
- [Complete Workflows](https://gillescolling.com/tulpaRatio/articles/workflows.html): four analyses from data to reported ratios: catch per unit effort, relative abundance, detection probability and temporal trends.
- [Spatial and Temporal Models](https://gillescolling.com/tulpaRatio/articles/spatial-temporal.html): areal fields, Gaussian processes, temporal and space-time terms.
- [Random Effects](https://gillescolling.com/tulpaRatio/articles/random-effects.html): shared, process-specific, nested and crossed random effects.
- [Zero-Inflation and Hurdle Models](https://gillescolling.com/tulpaRatio/articles/zero-inflation.html): numerators with excess zeros or ones.
- [Full reference](https://gillescolling.com/tulpaRatio/reference/): every function, grouped by job.

## Getting help

Questions and bug reports go to the [GitHub issues](https://github.com/gcol33/tulpaRatio/issues). A bug report is easiest to act on with a small reproducible example, for instance made with [reprex](https://reprex.tidyverse.org/).
